Age: 62
Sex: Male
Complaint: Progressive generalized weakness, muscle cramps, and palpitations after missing two hemodialysis sessions, with dietary intake of high‑potassium foods.
Analysis: This patient with stage 4 chronic kidney disease on maintenance hemodialysis presents with severe hyperkalemia (K 7.8 mEq/L) due to missed dialysis and continued dietary potassium intake (bananas, orange juice). ECG shows absent P waves, widened QRS (180 ms), peaked T waves, and an emerging sine wave pattern—a pre‑arrest rhythm indicating life‑threatening cardiac toxicity. Clinical findings of bradycardia, irregular pulse, diminished deep tendon reflexes, and hypertension are consistent with hyperkalemia. The primary differential is hyperkalemic cardiac arrhythmia; contributing factors include metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 14 mEq/L) and uremia. Emergent IV calcium gluconate was given to stabilize the myocardium.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Repeat serum potassium, continuous ECG monitoring, repeat ECG.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Nephrology
Recommendations: 1. Maintain continuous cardiac monitoring. 2. Administer IV insulin with dextrose and an inhaled beta‑agonist to temporarily shift potassium intracellularly. 3. Arrange emergent hemodialysis for definitive potassium removal. 4. Monitor serum potassium every 1–2 hours until stable. 5. Address transportation barriers to prevent future missed sessions. 6. Provide dietary counseling to avoid high‑potassium foods. 7. Manage hypertension and fluid overload with dialysis and antihypertensives as needed.
Notes: Calcium gluconate stabilizes the cardiac membrane but does not lower serum potassium; definitive treatment is hemodialysis. Watch for rebound hyperkalemia after initial transient shifts.

Vignette:
A 52-year-old obese man with a BMI of 36 presents for evaluation after his wife noticed he has been drinking large amounts of water and urinating frequently over the past several weeks. He reports increased thirst, frequent nighttime urination disrupting sleep, and a 10-pound unintentional weight loss over 2 months. He also describes blurry vision and increased fatigue. His past medical history includes hypertension treated with lisinopril and hyperlipidemia. Family history is significant for type 2 diabetes in both parents. He works a sedentary desk job and does not exercise regularly. Vital signs show blood pressure 144/92, heart rate 78. On examination, he is obese with acanthosis nigricans on the posterior neck and axillae. Foot examination shows intact sensation to monofilament and palpable pedal pulses. Fasting plasma glucose is 210 mg/dL, and HbA1c is 9.2%. Urinalysis shows glucosuria without ketonuria.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 52
Sex: Male
Complaint: Increased thirst, frequent urination (including nocturia), unintentional 10-pound weight loss over 2 months, blurry vision, and fatigue.
Analysis: This patient presents with classic hyperglycemic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, blurred vision) and diagnostic laboratory values (fasting glucose 210 mg/dL, HbA1c 9.2%). The presence of obesity (BMI 36), acanthosis nigricans, hypertension, family history of type 2 diabetes, and absence of ketonuria strongly supports a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus. The lack of ketonuria and stable vital signs help rule out diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. The blurry vision is likely due to osmotic lens changes and should improve with glycemic control. Hypertension is inadequately controlled on current therapy.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Fasting lipid panel, serum creatinine with eGFR, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and dilated eye examination.
Conclusion: Newly diagnosed, uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 9.2%) with associated obesity, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: Initiate lifestyle modifications (dietary counseling, regular physical activity, weight loss). Start metformin as first-line pharmacotherapy; consider additional glucose-lowering agents if needed to achieve target HbA1c. Intensify antihypertensive therapy (e.g., increase lisinopril or add another agent) to reach goal blood pressure. Refer to diabetes self-management education and medical nutrition therapy. Schedule ophthalmology evaluation for blurry vision and baseline retinal screening. Provide foot care education and encourage annual monofilament testing. Monitor for hypoglycemia and adjust therapy based on home glucose monitoring.
Notes: Blurry vision frequently resolves with improved glycemic control; patient should be counseled to avoid new glasses prescription until glucose stabilizes. Acanthosis nigricans may improve with weight loss and insulin sensitization. Follow-up in 2–4 weeks to assess response and tolerability.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old man with a known history of chronic rhinosinusitis and bilateral nasal polyps presents with a 10-day history of worsening facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion, and anosmia. He has had recurrent sinus infections averaging four to five times per year and has previously undergone polypectomy two years ago. He reports postnasal drip and a productive cough worse at night. He denies fever, visual changes, or severe headache. On examination, the nasal mucosa is edematous and erythematous bilaterally with visible polypoid tissue and mucopurulent drainage in the middle meatus. There is tenderness over the maxillary and frontal sinuses. Oropharynx shows cobblestoning of the posterior pharyngeal wall.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 40 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: 10-day history of worsening facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion, and anosmia in a patient with known chronic rhinosinusitis and bilateral nasal polyps.
Analysis: This patient with known chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps presents with an acute worsening of symptoms, including purulent discharge, tender sinuses, and mucopurulent drainage on examination, strongly suggesting an acute bacterial exacerbation. The absence of fever, severe headache, or visual changes argues against orbital or intracranial complications. Postnasal drip and cobblestoning point to an underlying allergic or inflammatory component. Differential considerations include acute bacterial rhinosinusitis superimposed on chronic disease, allergic fungal rhinosinusitis given the polyp history, or a simple viral exacerbation, but the purulence and focal tenderness favor a bacterial superinfection.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Acute exacerbation of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, likely bacterial superinfection.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Initiate empiric antibiotic therapy (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate) for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, continue intranasal corticosteroids and saline nasal irrigations. Consider a short course of oral steroids if significant mucosal edema is present. Schedule follow-up with otolaryngology for nasal endoscopy and long-term management of polyps. Address allergic rhinitis with oral antihistamines and environmental control measures if applicable. Advise the patient to return immediately if symptoms worsen, especially with vision changes, severe headache, or high fever.
Notes: If no improvement within 48-72 hours or if red flag symptoms develop, obtain a non-contrast CT of the sinuses to exclude complications or alternative diagnoses.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 35
Sex: male
Complaint: Progressive bilateral submandibular and sublingual swelling with trismus, odynophagia, muffled voice, and respiratory distress starting 3 days after lower left second molar extraction.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for Ludwig’s angina—a rapidly spreading cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, often odontogenic. Supporting findings include woody submandibular induration, floor-of-mouth elevation displacing the tongue, hot potato voice, trismus, inspiratory stridor, and hypoxia. CT demonstrates multiloculated fluid collections with airway narrowing. The primary threat is acute airway obstruction from soft tissue edema and abscess formation; sepsis is a secondary concern. The differential could include other deep neck space infections, but the bilateral involvement and rapid progression make Ludwig’s angina the leading diagnosis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Ludwig’s angina complicated by impending airway obstruction and systemic infection (fever, tachycardia, hypoxia).
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Secure the airway immediately—preferably via awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation in a controlled setting (e.g., operating room) with surgical backup (cricothyroidotomy/tracheostomy) if needed. Start intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics covering oral anaerobes and aerobes (e.g., ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin). Arrange urgent surgical drainage of the submandibular and sublingual abscesses once the airway is stabilized. Admit to an intensive care unit for close monitoring. Blood cultures and lactate level may guide sepsis management.
Notes: Deterioration can occur rapidly; keep the patient sitting upright, avoid supine positioning, and minimize airway instrumentation until definitive control is achieved.

Vignette:
A 24-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks gestation is brought in by ambulance after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting approximately 2 minutes. Her partner reports she has complained of a persistent headache, visual disturbances described as flashing lights, and swelling of her face and hands over the past 2 days. She did not attend her last two prenatal appointments. On examination, she is postictal, moaning, and not following commands. Vital signs: T 37.6C, HR 112, RR 22, BP 182/116, SpO2 94%. Significant periorbital and bilateral upper extremity edema is present. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ bilaterally with sustained clonus at the ankles. Fetal heart rate monitoring shows persistent late decelerations. Labs: platelets 92,000/mcL, AST 286 U/L, ALT 312 U/L, LDH 680 U/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 5.2. IV magnesium sulfate is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is planned.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 24
Sex: Female
Complaint: Witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at 36 weeks gestation, preceded by persistent headache, visual flashing lights, and facial/hand swelling; now postictal with severe hypertension, edema, hyperreflexia, clonus, and fetal distress.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for eclampsia superimposed on severe preeclampsia with HELLP syndrome. Strong supporting findings include severe hypertension (182/116 mmHg), significant proteinuria (UPCR 5.2), thrombocytopenia (92,000/mcL), elevated transaminases (AST 286 U/L, ALT 312 U/L), elevated LDH (680 U/L), acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.4 mg/dL), and neurological symptoms (headache, visual changes, seizure) with hyperreflexia and sustained clonus. Fetal late decelerations indicate uteroplacental insufficiency. The main differential includes other seizure etiologies (e.g., epilepsy, intracranial hemorrhage), but the preeclamptic laboratory and clinical profile makes eclampsia the overwhelming diagnosis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Eclampsia with severe features and HELLP syndrome at 36 weeks gestation, complicated by fetal distress, requiring immediate delivery.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology
Recommendations: Continue intravenous magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis with close monitoring for magnesium toxicity (respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes, urine output). Administer antihypertensive therapy (e.g., intravenous labetalol or hydralazine) to lower blood pressure to a safe range (e.g., <160/105 mmHg) while avoiding precipitous drops. Proceed with emergent cesarean delivery under appropriate anesthesia, with neonatal resuscitation team present. Postoperatively, monitor in an intensive care setting for worsening HELLP syndrome, renal failure, pulmonary edema, or further seizures. Avoid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs given thrombocytopenia and renal impairment.
Notes: Delivery is the definitive treatment for preeclampsia/eclampsia; magnesium sulfate should be continued for 24 hours postpartum.

Vignette:
A 34-year-old woman with no known underlying lung disease 12-day history of cough. She initially had nasal congestion and a mild sore throat, but now her symptoms are all related to a productive cough without paroxysms. She denies any sick contacts. On physical examination she is not in respiratory distress and is afebrile with normal vital signs. No signs of URI are noted. Scattered wheezes are present diffusely on lung auscultation.

Age: 34  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: 12-day productive cough without paroxysms, preceded by nasal congestion and mild sore throat; no sick contacts.  
Analysis: The history suggests a viral upper respiratory infection that has progressed to acute bronchitis or post-viral cough with bronchial hyperreactivity. Supportive findings include a productive cough of 12 days, absence of fever, normal vital signs, no respiratory distress, and no signs of upper respiratory infection on examination. Diffuse scattered wheezing suggests reactive airways or bronchospasm rather than focal pneumonia. Pertussis is less likely because there are no paroxysms and no known sick contacts.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Clinically consistent with acute bronchitis or post-viral cough with reactive airway wheezing; no signs of severe illness or pneumonia.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  
Recommendations: Manage as an outpatient with supportive care. Consider a short-acting bronchodilator for wheezing. Avoid routine antibiotics in the absence of fever, purulent sputum, or signs of bacterial infection. Reassess if symptoms worsen, dyspnea develops, or cough persists beyond the expected course.

Age: 24
Sex: Male
Complaint: Painful small bump in beard area 2 days after shaving against the grain.
Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with pseudofolliculitis barbae (ingrown hair). Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Discontinue shaving against the grain; switch to a single-blade razor or electric shaver. Apply warm compresses for 10–15 minutes several times a day to soften the skin and encourage the hair to emerge. If the hair loop is accessible, it may be gently lifted with a sterile needle after cleansing the area with alcohol. A topical over-the-counter antibiotic ointment can be applied if the skin surface is breached. Monitor for increasing pain, fluctuation, spreading redness, or fever; if these occur, seek medical evaluation.

First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.

Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,

Complaint: Follow-up for uncontrolled type 2 diabetes with hyperglycemia, polydipsia, and polyuria; HbA1c increased to 8.1% despite maximal oral therapy.

Differential includes inadequate pharmacotherapy, possible non-adherence, and need for alternative agents. Given obesity, cardiovascular risk factors, and neuropathy, a GLP-1 receptor agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor should be considered to improve glycemic control, promote weight loss, and provide cardiovascular/renal protection. Addressing needle fear is critical to enable injectable therapy if needed.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe left-sided pelvic pain and lightheadedness that began 45 minutes ago. She reports 7 weeks of amenorrhea and a positive home pregnancy test 5 days ago. She has a history of pelvic inflammatory disease and a prior left tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate 2 years ago. On examination, she is pale, diaphoretic, and appears acutely ill. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 132, RR 24, BP 78/48, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals diffuse lower abdominal tenderness with peritoneal signs. Pelvic exam demonstrates cervical motion tenderness and a tender left adnexal mass. Quantitative beta-hCG is 4,200 mIU/mL. Bedside transvaginal ultrasound reveals an empty uterus, a complex left adnexal mass with ring-of-fire sign, and significant free fluid in the pelvis and Morison's pouch. Hemoglobin returns at 7.8 g/dL. O-negative blood is ordered and the OR is alerted for emergent laparotomy.

Sex: Female
Complaint: Sudden severe left-sided pelvic pain, lightheadedness, 7 weeks amenorrhea, positive home pregnancy test.
Analysis: The patient has a high-risk history (prior ectopic, PID) and presents with acute pelvic pain, amenorrhea, positive beta-hCG, empty uterus, complex left adnexal mass with ring-of-fire sign, and significant free fluid extending to Morison’s pouch. Differential includes ruptured hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst, but the empty uterus, ring-of-fire sign, and profound shock strongly favor ruptured tubal ectopic.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (diagnosis is confirmed; immediate surgical intervention is required).

Notes: None

Vignette:
A 22-year-old female soccer player presents to the sports medicine clinic two days after sustaining a left knee injury during a game. She reports that while pivoting to change direction she felt a sudden pop in her knee followed by immediate swelling and inability to continue playing. She was unable to bear full weight and has been using crutches since. She denies any prior knee injuries. On examination, there is a moderate effusion of the left knee. Range of motion is limited by pain and swelling. The Lachman test is positive with a soft endpoint on the left, and the anterior drawer test demonstrates increased anterior tibial translation compared to the right. McMurray test is equivocal. The collateral ligaments are stable. She is neurovascularly intact distally.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 22
Sex: Female
Complaint: Acute left knee injury with a pop, immediate swelling, and inability to bear weight after pivoting during soccer.
Analysis: The history of a non-contact pivoting injury with an audible pop, rapid effusion, and inability to continue play is classic for an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear. Physical exam findings of a moderate effusion, positive Lachman test with a soft endpoint, and increased anterior tibial translation on anterior drawer strongly support an ACL rupture. The equivocal McMurray test raises the possibility of an associated meniscal tear but is not diagnostic. Stable collateral ligaments and intact neurovascular status argue against multi-ligament injury or neurovascular compromise. The main differential includes isolated ACL tear versus combined ACL and meniscal injury; patellar dislocation or fracture is less likely given the mechanism and ligamentous laxity.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the left knee (to confirm ACL tear, evaluate menisci, cartilage, and other soft tissues); weight-bearing radiographs (AP, lateral, Merchant views) may be considered to rule out fracture or loose bodies but are not strictly required if MRI is obtained.
Conclusion: High probability of acute complete left anterior cruciate ligament tear, with possible associated meniscal injury.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Continue non-weight-bearing with crutches, apply ice and compression to control swelling, and elevate the limb. Initiate early range-of-motion exercises as tolerated once pain and swelling subside. Refer to an orthopedic surgeon for definitive management, including discussion of surgical reconstruction versus conservative treatment based on MRI findings and patient’s activity level. Preoperative physical therapy (prehabilitation) to restore range of motion and quadriceps strength is advised. If meniscal tear is confirmed, address accordingly.

Sex: Male

Advise not sharing combs, hats, towels, or bedding, and evaluate close contacts or classmates given the reported similar cases. Follow up clinically to confirm hair regrowth and monitor for treatment side effects.

A 38-year-old male computer programmer presents with perianal discomfort and a small palpable lump that he noticed 3 days ago. baseline_protocol:
Age: 58
Sex: Male
Complaint: Large-volume hematemesis (bright red blood with clots) and melena over 2 days, with hypovolemic shock.
Analysis: The patient has decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis with known esophageal varices, non-compliant with propranolol prophylaxis. He presents with massive hematemesis and melena, indicating active upper gastrointestinal bleeding most likely from variceal rupture due to portal hypertension. Clinical findings of hemodynamic instability (tachycardia, hypotension, confusion), pallor, anemia (Hb 6.2 g/dL), thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy (INR 2.4), and elevated BUN support the diagnosis of acute variceal hemorrhage complicated by hemorrhagic shock and hepatic encephalopathy. Differential includes non-variceal upper GI bleed (e.g., peptic ulcer), but variceal origin is strongly favored by the history of cirrhosis, known varices, and severity of bleeding. Immediate intervention is required to control bleeding and prevent decompensation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urgent upper endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy) for diagnosis and therapeutic band ligation; continuous vital sign monitoring; pulse oximetry; type and crossmatch for blood products; possibly central venous catheter for resuscitation.
Conclusion: Acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage with hemorrhagic shock and hepatic encephalopathy in a patient with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class C).
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: Activate massive transfusion protocol with packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, and platelets; administer vasoactive drugs (e.g., octreotide or terlipressin) to reduce portal pressure; start prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone); perform urgent upper endoscopy for band ligation; manage hepatic encephalopathy with lactulose and rifaximin; admit to intensive care unit; correct coagulopathy; consider Sengstaken-Blakemore tube if endoscopic therapy fails; monitor for rebleeding and complications.
Notes: High mortality due to Child-Pugh C cirrhosis; risk of aspiration from ongoing hematemesis; non-compliance with propranolol may complicate long-term management; early involvement of liver transplant team if appropriate.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 50 years old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden collapse with limb shaking, drooling, and loss of consciousness; postictal confusion and lethargy.
Analysis: The witnessed episode of sudden collapse from a sitting position, limb shaking, drooling, and tongue laceration is consistent with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Postictal confusion and a subsequent period of severe bradycardia (30 bpm), hypotension (74/52 mm Hg), and bradypnea suggest autonomic instability or a transient rise in intracranial pressure. Recovery revealed a subtle left upper extremity dysdiadochokinesia, pointing to a right cerebellar or parietal lesion. The head CT is interpreted as showing an intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the right parietal area, which explains the acute seizure and focal neurologic sign. Differential considerations include ischemic stroke (less likely with acute CT hyperdensity), subarachnoid hemorrhage, or postictal cerebral edema. The punctate red spots on the leg may be petechiae from the fall or a bleeding tendency, possibly exacerbated by aspirin use.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CT head (already performed); MRI brain with susceptibility-weighted imaging to confirm hemorrhage and assess underlying lesions; CT or MR angiography if vascular malformation is suspected; EEG if ongoing subclinical seizures; coagulation studies (PT/PTT, platelet count); toxicology screen.
Conclusion: Intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the right parietal area presenting with new-onset seizure and focal neurologic deficit.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: Admit to intensive care unit for continuous neurologic and hemodynamic monitoring. Obtain urgent neurosurgery consultation for possible surgical evacuation or external ventricular drain if hydrocephalus develops. Manage blood pressure cautiously (target systolic 140–160 mm Hg) to prevent hematoma expansion while maintaining cerebral perfusion. Discontinue aspirin and consider platelet transfusion if clinically indicated. Initiate antiepileptic medication (e.g., levetiracetam) for seizure control. Perform MRI and vascular imaging to evaluate for underlying arteriovenous malformation, cavernoma, or cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Monitor for rebleeding, worsening edema, or herniation. Once stable, involve physical and occupational therapy for left upper extremity coordination deficits.
Notes: The transient bradycardia and hypotension episode warrants cardiac telemetry; if recurrent, consider neurogenic or vasovagal etiology. Aspirin use may have contributed to hemorrhage; avoid antiplatelet agents until the source is treated.

First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Vignette:
A 16-year-old male competitive swimmer presents with a 4-day history of progressive right ear pain and itching. He has been swimming daily for the past 3 weeks during summer training. The pain worsens when he chews food and when he lies on his right side. He reports a sensation of fullness in the ear and mild hearing reduction. He denies fever, ear discharge, or recent upper respiratory symptoms. On examination, vital signs are normal. There is marked tenderness on manipulation of the right tragus and with traction on the right auricle. Otoscopic examination reveals a narrowed, edematous external auditory canal with erythematous, macerated skin and scant white debris. The tympanic membrane is barely visible but appears intact. The left ear examination is normal. There is no periauricular lymphadenopathy, mastoid tenderness, or facial nerve dysfunction.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 16 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: 4-day history of progressive right ear pain, itching, ear fullness, and mild hearing reduction after daily swimming; pain worsens with chewing and lying on the right side.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with acute otitis externa, commonly known as swimmer's ear. Key supporting findings include recent prolonged daily swimming, right ear pain and itching, marked tenderness with tragus manipulation and auricle traction, and otoscopic evidence of a narrowed, edematous external auditory canal with erythematous, macerated skin and scant white debris. The tympanic membrane appears intact, and there is no fever, ear discharge, mastoid tenderness, periauricular lymphadenopathy, or facial nerve dysfunction, making complicated or necrotizing otitis externa unlikely. The main differential considerations include acute otitis media, contact dermatitis, fungal otitis externa, and a furuncle of the external canal; however, the canal findings and tragal/traction tenderness strongly favor acute otitis externa.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Uncomplicated acute otitis externa of the right ear in an otherwise healthy adolescent swimmer.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Keep the right ear dry and avoid swimming and water exposure until symptoms resolve. Use over-the-counter analgesia such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen for pain. Start a topical antibiotic-corticosteroid otic drop, typically a fluoroquinolone-containing preparation, after confirming the tympanic membrane appears intact. Avoid inserting cotton swabs or other objects into the ear. If the external auditory canal is too narrowed for drops to penetrate, referral to otolaryngology for possible wick placement may be needed. Arrange follow-up in 48–72 hours if there is no improvement or if pain, swelling, fever, or discharge develops. Oral antibiotics are not routinely indicated in this uncomplicated case without systemic signs or risk factors.
Notes: Tympanic membrane was barely visible but appeared intact on otoscopy; if perforation cannot be fully excluded, avoid potentially ototoxic ear drops and re-evaluate.

Vignette:
A 38-year-old man with no significant history of back pain developed acute LBP when lifting boxes 2 weeks ago. The pain is aching in nature, located in the left lumbar area, and associated with spasms. He describes previous similar episodes several years ago, which resolved without seeing a doctor. He denies any leg pain or weakness. He also denies fevers, chills, weight loss, and recent infections. Over-the-counter ibuprofen has helped somewhat, but he has taken it only twice a day for the past 3 days because he does not want to become dependent on painkillers. On examination, there is decreased lumbar flexion and extension secondary to pain, but a neurologic exam is unremarkable.

Age: 38
Sex: Male
Complaint: Acute low back pain after lifting boxes, aching, left lumbar area, with spasms, no leg pain or neurological symptoms.
Analysis: The presentation is consistent with acute mechanical low back pain, most likely a lumbar muscle strain given the lifting incident and localized pain with spasm. Absence of leg pain, weakness, or neurological deficits rules out radiculopathy or cauda equina syndrome. No red flags (fever, chills, weight loss, recent infection) make infection, malignancy, or fracture unlikely. Previous similar episodes resolved spontaneously, supporting a benign recurrent musculoskeletal pattern. Ibuprofen provides partial relief. Examination shows pain-limited range of motion but normal neurological findings, further confirming a non-neurological, mechanical etiology.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Acute mechanical low back pain, likely lumbar strain, without neurological involvement or red flags.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics

Apply local heat or cold as preferred. Maintain light activity and avoid bed rest; gentle stretching may help. Avoid heavy lifting, bending, and twisting. Return for evaluation if pain worsens, persists beyond 4–6 weeks, or if leg pain, weakness, numbness, or bowel/bladder symptoms develop.
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 30-year-old woman, 10 days postpartum after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, presents with sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath that began 2 hours ago while breastfeeding. She reports mild right calf swelling for the past 3 days that she attributed to normal postpartum changes. On examination, she is tachypneic and anxious. Vital signs: T 37.3C, HR 118, RR 26, BP 98/62, SpO2 91% on room air. Right calf is 3 cm larger in circumference than the left with a palpable cord. Lungs are clear. D-dimer is elevated at 4,200 ng/mL. CT pulmonary angiography reveals bilateral segmental and subsegmental pulmonary emboli with right heart strain.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 30-year-old woman
Sex: Female
Complaint: Sudden-onset right pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, and mild right calf swelling 10 days postpartum.
Analysis: The patient presents with classic features of pulmonary embolism (PE): acute pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and tachypnea in a postpartum woman with unilateral leg swelling. Strongest supporting facts include elevated D-dimer, CT pulmonary angiography confirmation of bilateral segmental/subsegmental emboli with right heart strain, tachycardia, borderline hypotension, and hypoxia. The postpartum state is a major risk factor for venous thromboembolism. The presence of right heart strain indicates a higher-risk PE. The main differential would include postpartum cardiomyopathy, amniotic fluid embolism (less likely at 10 days), or pneumonia, but the clinical picture and CT findings firmly establish the diagnosis of PE with right ventricular dysfunction.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Acute intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism with right heart strain in a postpartum woman, complicated by concomitant deep vein thrombosis of the right leg.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Immediate hospitalization, preferably in a monitored setting (ICU) for continuous telemetry and oxygen saturation monitoring. Start therapeutic anticoagulation (low-molecular-weight heparin or unfractionated heparin) unless contraindicated. Supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO₂ >90%. Obtain echocardiogram to assess right ventricular function and rule out other abnormalities. Send cardiac biomarkers (troponin, BNP/NT-proBNP) if not already done. Monitor for hemodynamic deterioration; if hypotension or shock develops, consider systemic thrombolysis or catheter-directed therapy. Manage DVT with limb elevation and advise against massage. Ensure anticoagulation is compatible with breastfeeding (LMWH or warfarin are generally safe). Provide analgesia for pleuritic pain as needed. Consult pulmonology and cardiology as appropriate. Consider thrombophilia evaluation postpartum, but not acutely. Early mobilization as tolerated and graduated compression stockings for the leg.
Notes: Despite clear lungs on auscultation, hypoxia persisted, requiring oxygen. The right calf swelling with palpable cord is clinically diagnostic for DVT, though confirmatory ultrasound could be deferred to avoid delay in anticoagulation. Right heart strain on CT is an independent predictor of poor outcome, underscoring the need for close monitoring.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 22
Sex: Male
Complaint: Severe respiratory distress, gasping, unable to speak in full sentences after high-speed motorcycle collision with right-sided impact.
Analysis: The patient presents with classic signs of tension pneumothorax: tracheal deviation to the left, distended neck veins, hyperresonance and absent breath sounds on the right, subcutaneous emphysema, severe hypoxia (SpO2 78% on 15L non-rebreather), and hypotension (BP 74/48) with tachycardia (HR 138). The immediate rush of air upon needle decompression confirms the diagnosis and provides temporary relief. The hypotension and tachycardia likely reflect obstructive shock from the tension pneumothorax, but concomitant hemorrhagic shock from other injuries cannot be excluded. The mechanism (high-speed motorcycle collision, thrown, striking guardrail) raises concern for additional thoracic or abdominal trauma.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Chest X-ray (post-decompression), CT trauma series (chest/abdomen/pelvis) if hemodynamically stable, focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST), continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring.
Conclusion: Tension pneumothorax secondary to blunt thoracic trauma, temporarily relieved by needle decompression; requires definitive chest tube placement and evaluation for other injuries.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Immediately place a right-sided tube thoracostomy (chest tube) to prevent recurrence of tension pneumothorax. Continue high-flow oxygen and reassess SpO2. Establish large-bore IV access and begin fluid resuscitation for hypotension, while monitoring for response. Obtain a portable chest X-ray to confirm lung re-expansion and tube position. Once stabilized, perform CT trauma series to evaluate for pulmonary contusion, hemothorax, great vessel injury, rib fractures, and intra-abdominal injuries. Admit to surgical ICU or trauma service for ongoing monitoring.
Notes: Needle decompression is a temporizing measure; definitive management requires tube thoracostomy. Persistent hypotension after decompression should prompt search for other sources of shock (e.g., tension pneumothorax recurrence, massive hemothorax, cardiac tamponade, or intra-abdominal hemorrhage).

Age: 48-year-old
Sex: male
Complaint: Sharp stabbing right heel pain, worst with first steps in the morning and after prolonged sitting, aggravated by extended walking on pavement, without trauma or neurological symptoms.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for plantar fasciitis: focal tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle, positive windlass test, morning start-up pain, and tight gastrocnemius-soleus complex. Occupational factors (daily 8-mile walking on pavement, non-supportive work boots) and obesity (BMI 31) are strong contributing factors. Differential diagnoses such as fat pad atrophy, tarsal tunnel syndrome, or stress fracture are less likely given the absence of neurological signs, normal heel pad, and characteristic mechanical pain pattern.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Right plantar fasciitis secondary to repetitive overload, obesity, tight calf muscles, and inadequate footwear.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Initiate conservative management: rest and activity modification (reduce walking distance, avoid barefoot walking), ice massage, daily calf-stretching exercises (gastrocnemius and soleus), and use of over-the-counter heel cups or arch-supporting orthotic inserts in work boots. Consider night splint to maintain dorsiflexion. Weight loss counseling. Short course of NSAIDs if not contraindicated. If no improvement in 6–8 weeks, refer for physical therapy or consider corticosteroid injection. Address footwear: replace worn boots and ensure proper cushioning.
Notes: The calcaneal spur is a common incidental finding and does not require intervention; treatment targets the plantar fascia and biomechanical factors.

Vignette:
A 45-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with a 6-month history of progressive fatigue, weight gain of 15 pounds despite no change in diet, constipation, cold intolerance, and dry skin. She reports her hair has become thin and brittle and she has noticed puffiness around her eyes in the morning. Her menstrual periods have become heavier and more irregular. She has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. Family history is positive for thyroid disease in her mother and sister. Vital signs show heart rate 56, blood pressure 136/88, temperature 97.2°F. On examination, she appears sluggish. Skin is cool, dry, and pale. There is periorbital edema and non-pitting edema of the lower extremities. The thyroid gland is diffusely enlarged without nodules. Deep tendon reflexes show delayed relaxation phase. TSH is markedly elevated at 48 mIU/L and free T4 is low at 0.4 ng/dL. Anti-TPO antibodies are positive.

The family history of thyroid disease supports an autoimmune etiology. No alternative diagnosis is suggested by the case.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Primary hypothyroidism due to Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: Initiate levothyroxine replacement therapy at a weight-based dose (e.g., 1.6 mcg/kg/day). Reassess clinically and check TSH in 6–8 weeks, adjusting dose as needed to achieve euthyroidism. Educate the patient on the lifelong nature of treatment, the importance of consistent daily intake on an empty stomach, and symptoms of over- or under-replacement. Monitor for resolution of symptoms and signs. Consider thyroid ultrasound if the goiter persists or changes. Advise on diet and exercise for weight management once euthyroid.
Notes: None

baseline_protocol:
Age: 48-year-old
Sex: Female
Complaint: Altered mental status with acute disorientation, somnolence, scleral icterus, right upper quadrant tenderness, and asterixis.
Analysis: The patient presents with acute liver failure (ALT 6498 U/L, total bilirubin 5.6 mg/dL, INR 6.8, and hepatic encephalopathy with asterixis and altered mental status) in the setting of excessive acetaminophen ingestion from multiple acetaminophen-containing preparations plus additional 500 mg pills. The extremely high transaminases, jaundice, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy strongly point to acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity. The main differential includes other causes of acute liver failure (viral, ischemic, autoimmune, Wilson disease), but the history of supratherapeutic acetaminophen use makes this the most likely diagnosis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serum acetaminophen level, comprehensive toxicology screen, viral hepatitis panel, abdominal ultrasound with Doppler, serum ammonia, arterial blood gas with lactate, repeat comprehensive metabolic panel, and coagulation studies.
Conclusion: Acute liver failure secondary to acetaminophen toxicity with hepatic encephalopathy.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: Immediately initiate N-acetylcysteine (NAC) protocol (intravenous loading dose followed by maintenance infusion). Provide supportive care and monitor for signs of cerebral edema. Administer vitamin K; consider fresh frozen plasma only if active bleeding or before invasive procedures. Contact a liver transplant center for evaluation. Vignette:
A 48-year-old male factory worker presents with a long-standing history of chronic low back pain that has worsened over the past 3 weeks with new radiating pain down the left posterior thigh and calf to the lateral foot. He describes the pain as sharp and shooting, rated 7 out of 10, aggravated by prolonged sitting and forward bending. He has been lifting heavy machinery parts for over 20 years. He denies bowel or bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, or fever. On examination, he has a positive straight leg raise on the left at 40 degrees. Decreased ankle reflex on the left is noted. Sensation to light touch is diminished over the lateral aspect of the left foot. Motor strength is 4 out of 5 in left ankle dorsiflexion.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 48
Sex: Male
Complaint: Chronic low back pain with acute worsening and new left-sided radicular pain in an L5 distribution (posterior thigh, calf, lateral foot).
Analysis: The patient’s long history of heavy lifting and chronic low back pain, combined with acute-onset sharp, shooting pain radiating along the left L5 dermatome, strongly suggests a lumbar disc herniation causing L5 radiculopathy. Key physical exam findings—positive straight leg raise at 40°, decreased ankle reflex, diminished sensation on the lateral foot, and weak ankle dorsiflexion—localize the lesion to the L5 nerve root. The absence of bowel/bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, or fever makes cauda equina syndrome or infection unlikely. Differential considerations include degenerative disc disease with acute herniation, lumbar spinal stenosis, or foraminal stenosis, but the acute radicular picture is most consistent with disc herniation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI lumbar spine (non-contrast)
Conclusion: Acute left L5 radiculopathy likely due to lumbar disc herniation superimposed on chronic occupational low back pain.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Obtain an MRI of the lumbar spine to confirm the level and extent of nerve root compression. Initiate pharmacotherapy with NSAIDs and a neuropathic pain agent (e.g., gabapentin). Advise activity modification, avoid heavy lifting and prolonged sitting, and refer for physical therapy. Arrange a spine surgery or orthopedic consultation for further management, including possible epidural steroid injection. Educate the patient on red-flag symptoms (progressive weakness, bowel/bladder changes) that would require immediate re-evaluation.
Notes: None

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 75-year-old woman presents with severe, diffuse abdominal pain of sudden onset 4 hours ago. She describes the pain as 10/10, constant, and poorly localized. Her past medical history includes atrial fibrillation (on apixaban), congestive heart failure, and hypertension. She recently self-discontinued her anticoagulation. On examination, she appears acutely distressed and diaphoretic. Vital signs: T 37.6C, HR 112 (irregularly irregular), RR 24, BP 102/64, SpO2 95%. Remarkably, abdominal examination reveals only mild diffuse tenderness with no guarding or rebound despite her severe pain level. Bowel sounds are hypoactive. Labs: WBC 18,400/mcL, lactate 6.2 mmol/L, LDH 520 U/L. CT angiography of the abdomen reveals a filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery consistent with acute embolus.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 75
Sex: Female
Complaint: Severe, sudden-onset diffuse abdominal pain (10/10, constant, poorly localized) for 4 hours, with atrial fibrillation and recent self-discontinuation of apixaban.
Analysis: The pain severity is out of proportion to the benign abdominal exam (mild tenderness, no guarding or rebound), which is classic for acute mesenteric ischemia. Risk factors include atrial fibrillation (embolic source) and recent anticoagulation cessation. Elevated lactate (6.2 mmol/L), LDH, WBC, hypotension, tachycardia, and CT angiography showing an SMA filling defect confirm acute embolic superior mesenteric artery occlusion. Differential diagnoses such as perforation, pancreatitis, or obstruction are excluded by imaging. The presentation mandates urgent intervention to prevent bowel infarction and sepsis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Acute superior mesenteric artery embolism causing acute mesenteric ischemia, likely cardioembolic from atrial fibrillation in the setting of discontinued anticoagulation.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: 1. Immediate surgical consultation for embolectomy and/or bowel resection. 2. Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics. 3. Consider reversal of any residual anticoagulant effect and start unfractionated heparin infusion if no contraindication. 4. Continuous monitoring for signs of bowel necrosis, sepsis, and hemodynamic instability. 5. Cardiology evaluation for atrial fibrillation management and long-term anticoagulation planning. 6. Address the self-discontinuation of apixaban through patient education and support.
Notes: The irregularly irregular pulse and history of atrial fibrillation underscore the need for rate control. Bowel viability assessment is time-critical; delayed intervention increases mortality. Once the acute episode resolves, a structured plan to resume anticoagulation is essential to prevent recurrence.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 20-yr-old woman comes to the office because of a 1-wk history of a feeling she describes as
"novocaine wearing off" extending from her waist to her toes on both sides of her body. She
says this feeling has been worsening. She has had no prior viral illness and has not received
any recent vaccinations or had any recent injuries. She has no weakness in her arms or legs,
but says she may be tripping more than usual; however, she has not fallen. She thinks her
fingertips feel "funny" as well. She has no headache, face pain, face numbness, double vision,
or other visual complaints. She does not have dysarthria, dysphasia, or difficulty swallowing.
She says that when wiping her perineal region, it feels "funny." She had an episode of left leg
numbness 2 yr ago that lasted 3 wk and that resolved by itself.

Review of Systems:
General: She has felt well until this current episode began and has had no fevers, chills, or
recent weight loss.

Skin: No rash or lesions.

HEENT: Noncontributory

Pulmonary: Noncontributory

Cardiovascular: Born with double outlet right ventricle, corrected at birth, then stented in 2005
because of residual scarring. Gets annual cardiology check-ups.

Gastrointestinal: Noncontributory

Genitourinary: Normal bladder and bowel function. Last menstrual period was 2 wk ago.

Musculoskeletal: No pain in neck, back, or joints.

Neurologic: See previous screen (History of Present Illness).

Psychiatric: She says her mood and general spirits have been good until this current.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Migraine headaches several times per year, last episode 4 mo prior.

Surgical history: Born with double outlet right ventricle, corrected at birth, then stented in 2005
because of residual scarring. Gets annual cardiology check-ups.

Medications: None

Allergies: None

Family history: Noncontributory

Social history: Regular diet, does not exercise. No history of recent travel. No drug, alcohol, or
tobacco use. Immunizations up-to-date, no recent exposure to illness. Sexually active with one
partner; uses condoms consistently.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Young woman in no apparent distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 75 beats/min
BP: 120/80 mm Hg
Respirations: 12/min

Skin: Warm, dry; no erythema or rash.

HEENT: Unremarkable

Pulmonary: Unremarkable

Cardiovascular: Unremarkable

Gastrointestinal: Unremarkable

Genitourinary: Unremarkable

Musculoskeletal: No visible or palpable lesions or tenderness along spine. Joints nontender, full
range of motion.

Neurologic:
Cranial nerves: 2 through 12 intact
Motor exam: Strength and muscle tone normal in both upper and both lower extremities. No
muscle atrophy or abnormal movements seen.
Sensory exam: Sensation intact bilaterally to light touch, pinprick, temperature, vibration, and
joint position
Reflexes: Normoactive and symmetric throughout
Coordination: Normal
Gait and balance: Normal
Detailed movement exam: Normal
Rectal examination: Normal perineal sensation and normal rectal sphincter tone

Mental status: Alert, oriented x3. Normal affect. Euthymic mood. Normal memory, judgment,
and insight.
*

baseline_protocol:
Age: 20  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: One-week history of progressive "novocaine wearing off" sensation from waist down bilaterally, unusual fingertip and perineal feelings, possible increased tripping, without weakness or sphincter dysfunction; prior episode of self‑resolved left leg numbness 2 years ago.  
Analysis: The history of a subacute ascending sensory disturbance (band‑like waist‑to‑toes paresthesias) with distal and perineal involvement suggests a spinal cord lesion, likely a transverse myelitis. The past episode of left leg numbness that resolved spontaneously supports a recurring demyelinating process. The current normal neurological examination does not exclude early myelitis. The MRI images (reviewed) demonstrate findings consistent with demyelinating plaques in the cervical/thoracic spine and brain, fulfilling dissemination in space. Together with the temporal separation, the presentation meets diagnostic criteria for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. No red flags for infection, vascular compromise, or cord compression are present.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None; MRI already obtained is sufficient for initial diagnosis. Lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands may be considered in equivocal cases but is not mandatory here.  
Conclusion: Relapsing‑remitting multiple sclerosis presenting with sensory spinal cord relapse.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Neurology  
Recommendations: Refer to neurologist for confirmation and initiation of disease-modifying therapy. Educate the patient about the diagnosis, prognosis, and early treatment benefits. Address symptom management (e.g., neuropathic pain if needed). Monitor for new relapses or progression. Repeat neurological exam in follow‑up. No immediate emergency intervention is indicated.  
Notes: The normal examination likely reflects a purely sensory relapse; however, careful monitoring for motor or autonomic involvement is warranted.

Vignette: A 10-day-old female neonate is brought in by her parents who report that she has been feeding poorly since yesterday, taking only half of her usual breast milk volume, and seems increasingly sleepy and difficult to arouse. tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[2]
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

[3]
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[4]
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[5]
tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

Vital signs: T 35.6C (rectal, hypothermic), HR 196, RR 62 with intermittent grunting, BP 48/28, SpO2 90% on room air. Skin is mottled with a grayish hue and capillary refill is 4 seconds. The fontanelle is flat. She is hypotonic with poor suck and grasp reflexes. Labs: WBC 3,200/mcL (leukopenia) with 28% bands, CRP 6.8 mg/dL, glucose 34 mg/dL, platelets 68,000/mcL, lactate 5.4 mmol/L. baseline_protocol:
Age: 10 days
Sex: Female
Complaint: Poor feeding, increased sleepiness, and difficult arousal since yesterday in a 10-day-old neonate.
Analysis: The neonate presents with clinical and laboratory findings consistent with septic shock: lethargy, weak high-pitched cry, hypothermia (35.6°C), tachycardia, tachypnea with grunting, hypotension, hypoxemia, mottled skin, delayed capillary refill, leukopenia with bandemia (28% bands), elevated CRP, hypoglycemia, thrombocytopenia, and lactic acidosis. Maternal GBS-positive status is a significant risk factor despite intrapartum antibiotics. The flat fontanelle and hypotonia raise concern for possible central nervous system involvement. The combination of perinatal risk, systemic inflammatory response, and hemodynamic instability strongly supports a diagnosis of late-onset neonatal sepsis, most likely bacterial (e.g., GBS, E. coli, Listeria). Other differentials such as congenital heart disease or inborn errors of metabolism are less likely given the infectious markers and acute deterioration.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiorespiratory monitor, pulse oximeter, non-invasive blood pressure monitoring; point-of-care glucose and lactate testing; repeat blood gas analysis; chest radiograph if respiratory distress persists; echocardiogram if cardiac function is questioned.
Conclusion: Neonatal septic shock secondary to late-onset bacterial sepsis in a neonate with maternal GBS colonization, presenting with hypothermia, hypotension, and multi-organ dysfunction.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Continue empiric ampicillin and gentamicin pending culture results. Provide respiratory support with supplemental oxygen; escalate to CPAP or mechanical ventilation if grunting, hypoxemia, or apnea worsen. Administer fluid resuscitation with 10–20 mL/kg normal saline boluses and consider vasopressors (e.g., dopamine) for persistent hypotension. Correct hypoglycemia with IV dextrose (2–4 mL/kg D10W bolus, then continuous infusion). Maintain thermoregulation in an incubator or radiant warmer. Monitor for seizures and consider continuous EEG if encephalopathy persists. Repeat blood, urine, and CSF cultures if no clinical improvement in 24–48 hours. Involve pediatric infectious disease and neonatology teams early.
Notes: Despite intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, GBS infection can still occur; maintain high suspicion for meningitis and adjust antibiotics (e.g., add cefotaxime) if CSF results indicate CNS involvement. Strict infection control and close hemodynamic monitoring are essential.

Vignette: A 65-year-old woman presents with recurring episodes of painful cramping in her right calf that wake her from sleep, occurring 2 to 3 times per week for the past month. There is no varicosity, skin discoloration, or warmth. Neurological examination of the lower extremities is unremarkable.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 65-year-old woman presents with recurring episodes of painful cramping in her right calf that wake her from sleep, occurring 2 to 3 times per week for the past month. Each episode lasts a few minutes and resolves with stretching or walking. She takes hydrochlorothiazide for mild hypertension. She denies leg swelling, skin color changes, or daytime calf pain. On examination, vital signs are normal. Both calves are non-tender, symmetric in size, and without edema. Peripheral pulses are intact bilaterally. There is no varicosity, skin discoloration, or warmth. Neurological examination of the lower extremities is unremarkable.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 65
Sex: Female
Complaint: Recurring painful nocturnal cramping in the right calf, waking from sleep, relieved by stretching or walking.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with benign nocturnal leg cramps. Key supporting features include age, unilateral calf cramps occurring exclusively at night, relief with stretching or walking, and normal physical examination (no edema, tenderness, vascular or neurological deficits). The use of hydrochlorothiazide, a thiazide diuretic, raises the possibility of electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) as a contributing factor. The absence of daytime claudication, skin changes, and intact peripheral pulses makes peripheral artery disease unlikely. Restless legs syndrome is less likely given the cramping quality and relief with movement, rather than an urge to move. No red flags for deep vein thrombosis or neurological disorders are present.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serum electrolytes (potassium, magnesium), possibly renal function panel.
Conclusion: Nocturnal leg cramps, likely exacerbated by hydrochlorothiazide-induced electrolyte imbalance.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: 1. Advise on calf-stretching exercises before bedtime and during cramps. 2. Ensure adequate hydration. 3. Check serum potassium and magnesium levels; if low, consider supplementation and/or adjustment of antihypertensive therapy (e.g., switching to a non-diuretic agent or adding a potassium-sparing diuretic). 4. Reassess in follow-up to monitor symptom frequency and electrolyte status. 5. If cramps persist despite correction of electrolytes, consider other causes (e.g., lumbar spine pathology) but no immediate imaging is indicated.
Notes: None

The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 54
Sex: Female
Complaint: Severe occipital headache, blurred vision, and progressive confusion for 4 hours.
Analysis: The patient presents with a hypertensive emergency (BP 238/142) causing end-organ damage. Neurological findings (confusion, hyperreflexia, bilateral Babinski) and CT evidence of posterior white matter edema are consistent with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). Fundoscopic papilledema, flame hemorrhages, and cotton-wool spots indicate grade IV hypertensive retinopathy. Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease (creatinine 3.8 from baseline 1.6, proteinuria, RBC casts) further supports malignant hypertension. The abrupt cessation of antihypertensives is the likely trigger. Differential includes hemorrhagic stroke (excluded by CT) and other encephalopathies, but the clinical picture strongly points to hypertensive emergency with PRES.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Hypertensive emergency with PRES, acute-on-chronic kidney injury, and grade IV hypertensive retinopathy.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Admit to ICU for continuous BP monitoring and gradual controlled reduction (no more than 25% in the first hour) using IV labetalol or nicardipine; avoid nitroprusside if possible due to renal impairment. Obtain emergent nephrology consultation. Restart oral antihypertensives once stable. Monitor neurological status and renal function closely. Address medication non-adherence before discharge.
Notes: PRES is typically reversible with prompt BP control; avoid overcorrection to prevent cerebral hypoperfusion.

Diagnosis10cm: Traumatic compartment syndrome of right lower extremity, initial encounter
Vignette: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after a skiing accident in which he sustained a closed tibial shaft fracture of the right leg, which was splinted in the field by ski patrol. He reports that his pain has been escalating dramatically despite receiving IV morphine 10 mg total, which is atypical for the degree of injury. He describes the pain as deep and burning, significantly worse with any passive movement of his right toes. On examination, the right lower leg appears tense and swollen within the splint. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 108, RR 20, BP 142/88, SpO2 99%. After splint removal, the anterior compartment of the right leg is firm and exquisitely tender. Pain is markedly worsened with passive extension of the right toes. Sensation is diminished in the first web space (deep peroneal nerve distribution). Dorsalis pedis pulse is still palpable but diminished compared to the left. Compartment pressure measurement reveals 48 mmHg in the anterior compartment (diastolic BP 88, delta pressure 40 mmHg). Orthopedic surgery is consulted for emergent four-compartment fasciotomy.
